primaryMeaning: Built on ilāh, 'one who is worshipped'. Classical scholars give several origins: aliha, 'to worship'; aliha, 'to be bewildered', since minds are left in awe before Him; and waliha, 'to turn to someone out of longing or need'. Many hold that Allah is al-ilāh, 'the God', joined into one name, while others hold it is a proper name not derived from any root.
extendedMeaning: Ilāh means any object of worship, true or false, so its plural āliha is used for the idols people took as gods: 'Do you take idols as gods (ālihatan)?' (6:74).
quranUsage: The most frequent root in the Quran (2,851 times), almost always as the name Allah, which begins the Basmala heading every surah except At-Tawbah (1:1). The common noun ilāh, 'god', carries the declaration of oneness: lā ilāha illā huwa, 'there is no god but He' (2:163, 2:255).

primaryMeaning: To say or speak. Qawl is a meaningful utterance — words put together to express something — and the root keeps to this single sense.
extendedMeaning: Qawl is also judged: believers are told to 'speak a word that is straight (qawlan sadīdā)' (33:70). Qīla, 'it was said', is used when the speaker is left unnamed (2:11).
quranUsage: Occurs 1,722 times. Qāla, 'he said', appears over 500 times and carries the Quran's many dialogues between Allah, the angels, prophets and their peoples (first at 2:30). The command qul, 'Say!', addressed to the Prophet, appears over 300 times, as in qul huwa Allāhu aḥad, 'Say: He is Allah, the One' (112:1).

primaryMeaning: To be, to come into being, to happen. From it come kawn, 'existence' or 'the universe', and makān, 'place' — where something comes to be.
quranUsage: Occurs 1,390 times, most often as kāna, 'was'. Used of Allah, kāna describes a permanent quality rather than a past one: wa kāna Allāhu ghafūran raḥīmā means 'Allah is ever Forgiving, Merciful' (4:96). The creative command kun fa-yakūn, 'Be, and it is', comes from this root (2:117).

primaryMeaning: To own, look after, and raise something stage by stage until it is complete. Al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī defines the root's core as tarbiya, bringing a thing to its fullness step by step. Rabb is the master who both owns and nurtures; the same root gives rabība, a stepdaughter raised in one's home (4:23).
extendedMeaning: Used of people, rabb means an owner or master: Yusuf asks to be mentioned to the king with 'mention me before your master (rabbika)' (12:42).
quranUsage: Occurs 980 times, nearly always as Rabb, 'Lord', usually with a possessive: rabbika 'your Lord', rabbī 'my Lord', and rabbanā 'our Lord', which opens many of the Quran's prayers, such as rabbanā ātinā fī al-dunyā ḥasanah, 'Our Lord, give us good in this world' (2:201). The first description of Allah in Al-Fātiḥah is rabb al-ʿālamīn, 'Lord of the worlds' (1:2).

primaryMeaning: To be safe and free of fear. Ibn Fāris gives two closely linked senses: trustworthiness (amāna), whose meaning is the heart being at rest, and affirming something as true. Āmana, 'to believe', is to trust in someone and so be secure with them.
extendedMeaning: Amāna, 'the trust', is what the heavens, the earth and the mountains declined to bear and man took on (33:72). Amn, 'security', describes the sanctuary of Makkah: 'whoever enters it shall be safe (āminan)' (3:97).
quranUsage: Occurs 879 times, most often as āmanū, 'they believed' (over 250 times), including the address yā ayyuhā alladhīna āmanū, 'O you who believe' (first at 2:104), and as mu'min, 'believer'. Al-Mu'min, 'the Giver of Security', is a name of Allah (59:23).

primaryMeaning: A mark or sign that sets something apart and makes it recognisable (ʿalam: a signpost, a banner). 'To know' (ʿalima) grows from this: knowing a thing is recognising it by its marks.
extendedMeaning: Allah 'taught (ʿallama) Adam the names of all things' (2:31). ʿIlm, 'knowledge', is what raises people in rank: 'Are those who know equal to those who do not know?' (39:9).
quranUsage: Occurs 854 times, mostly as verbs of knowing: yaʿlamūna 'they know', yaʿlamu 'He knows'. ʿAlīm, 'All-Knowing', describes Allah about 160 times (first at 2:29). Al-ʿālamīn, 'the worlds', appears in the opening praise of Al-Fātiḥah (1:2); classical scholars explain it as everything by which its Creator is known.

primaryMeaning: To stand up, and from that, to stand firm, to set something upright, and to take charge of it. Qawm, 'a people', is classically explained as those who stand together in each other's affairs.
extendedMeaning: Al-ṣirāṭ al-mustaqīm, 'the straight path', is the path that stands upright without bending (1:6). Al-Qayyūm, 'the Self-Sustaining', who holds all things up, is a name of Allah (2:255).
quranUsage: Occurs 660 times. Most common is qawm, 'people' (over 380 times), including the prophets' appeal yā qawmi, 'O my people' (7:59). Yawm al-qiyāma, 'the Day of Resurrection' — literally 'of standing up' — occurs 70 times (first at 2:85). Aqāma al-ṣalāh, 'to establish the prayer', means performing it upright and in full (2:3).

primaryMeaning: Āya is a clear sign or mark that points to something beyond itself. This root also groups the words ayy, 'which?', and ayyuhā, used after yā to call someone ('O you…'); these are related in form rather than in meaning.
quranUsage: Occurs 597 times. Āya, 'sign' (over 380 times), is used for the verses of the Quran, for the miracles given to prophets, and for signs in nature: 'In the creation of the heavens and the earth … are signs (la-āyātin) for people of understanding' (3:190). The call yā ayyuhā, 'O you', occurs about 160 times, as in yā ayyuhā al-nās, 'O mankind' (2:21).

primaryMeaning: To come. Its causative form ātā means 'to make something come', and so 'to bring' or 'to give'.
quranUsage: Occurs 549 times. As 'come', it describes messengers, punishment and the Hour arriving: 'The command of Allah has come (atā)' (16:1). As 'give', it describes Allah giving scripture and proofs — 'We gave (ātaynā) Musa the Book' (2:87) — and the command wa ātū al-zakāh, 'and give the zakah' (2:43).

primaryMeaning: To cover or conceal. A farmer covering seed with soil was called kāfir, and night was described the same way because it covers everything in darkness.
extendedMeaning: The literal sense survives in 57:20, where al-kuffār are 'the tillers' who admire the growth of their crops. Kaffāra, 'expiation', is what covers over a sin (5:89).
quranUsage: Occurs 525 times, mostly for covering over the truth by rejecting it, as in kafarū, 'they disbelieved' (over 190 times, first at 2:6). It is also used for ingratitude — covering over a blessing: 'if you are ungrateful (kafartum), My punishment is severe' (14:7).

primaryMeaning: To be separate or apart. From 'being apart' come bayna, 'between' — the gap separating two things — and bāna, 'to become clear', since a thing is clear when it stands apart from everything around it.
quranUsage: Occurs 523 times, as the preposition bayna, 'between', and in words of clarity: mubīn, 'clear' or 'making clear', often describing the Quran — 'a light and a clear Book (kitābun mubīn)' (5:15); bayyināt, 'clear proofs', brought by the messengers (2:87); and bayān, 'clear expression', which Allah taught mankind (55:4).

primaryMeaning: To will or want something. Shay', 'a thing', comes from the same root; grammarians explain it as 'what may be willed', or anything that can be known and spoken about.
extendedMeaning: The phrase in shā' Allāh, 'if Allah wills', is taught in 18:23–24: 'Never say of anything, "I will do that tomorrow," without adding "if Allah wills".'
quranUsage: Occurs 519 times. Shay' appears in the refrain inna Allāha ʿalā kulli shay'in qadīr, 'Allah has power over all things' (2:20). Shā'a, 'to will', expresses Allah's will, on which human will depends: 'You do not will unless Allah wills' (81:29).

primaryMeaning: To send forth, to let something go. The root carries a sense of gentle, continuous release: loose-flowing hair was called rasl, and camels arriving in successive groups came arsālan.
extendedMeaning: Risāla, 'message' or 'mission', is what a messenger delivers: Salih tells his people, 'I conveyed to you the message (risālata) of my Lord' (7:79).
quranUsage: Occurs 513 times: arsalnā, 'We sent', for Allah sending messengers, and rasūl, 'messenger' — one who carries a message on another's behalf. 'Allah and His Messenger' recurs throughout, as in 'whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger (rasūlahu)' (4:13). Winds too are 'sent' as bearers of good news (7:57).

primaryMeaning: A day. Beyond daylight or a full day and night, yawm is used for any period in which something takes place, especially a decisive event — the 'days' of the Arabs (ayyām al-ʿArab) were their famous battles.
extendedMeaning: The Quran speaks of days of a different measure: 'a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of what you count' (22:47).
quranUsage: Occurs 475 times, most often for the Last Day: yawm al-dīn, 'the Day of Judgment' (1:4), yawm al-qiyāma, 'the Day of Resurrection', and al-yawm al-ākhir, 'the Last Day' (2:62). Yawma'idhin, 'on that Day', points back to it throughout the later surahs.

primaryMeaning: The earth: the ground beneath one's feet, and by extension a land or country. Ibn Fāris relates it to whatever is low and lies beneath, as opposed to samā', what is high.
quranUsage: Occurs 461 times, very often paired with the heavens: al-samāwāt wa al-arḍ, 'the heavens and the earth' (2:255). It can mean the whole earth, on which Allah places man as a successor (khalīfa, 2:30), or a particular land, as when Musa tells his people to enter 'the holy land' (5:21).

primaryMeaning: To be high, to rise above. Samā', 'sky', is everything above you — classically even a ceiling or rain could be called samā'. The grammarians of Basra derived ism, 'name', from this root, since a name raises a thing into notice; those of Kufa derived it from w-s-m, 'mark'.
extendedMeaning: Al-asmā' al-ḥusnā, 'the most beautiful names', belong to Allah: 'call on Him by them' (7:180).
quranUsage: Occurs 381 times, mostly as al-samāwāt, 'the heavens', and al-samā', 'the sky'. Ism, 'name', begins every Basmala: bismi Allāh, 'In the name of Allah' (1:1). Musamman, 'named' or 'fixed', describes an appointed term (2:282).

primaryMeaning: To surround or encompass on all sides. Kull, 'all' or 'every', is the whole that takes in each of its parts. The same root gives iklīl, a crown encircling the head, and kalāla, a person who dies leaving neither parent nor child, whose heirs surround him from the sides.
extendedMeaning: Kalāla appears in the inheritance rulings (4:12, 4:176).
quranUsage: Occurs 377 times, mostly as kull: 'Every soul (kullu nafsin) will taste death' (3:185) and 'Allah has power over all things (kulli shay'in)' (2:20). Kullamā, 'whenever', is from this root too (2:20).

primaryMeaning: Classical scholars give more than one origin for ʿadhāb, 'punishment'. Some link it to ʿadhaba, 'to hold back', since punishment restrains the wrongdoer; al-Rāghib also mentions ʿadhb, 'fresh, sweet water', explaining punishment as taking the sweetness out of life.
extendedMeaning: The sense of sweet water appears when two seas meet: 'this one fresh and sweet (ʿadhbun furāt), and this one salty and bitter' (25:53).
quranUsage: Occurs 373 times, almost always as ʿadhāb, 'punishment', often with a description: ʿadhābun ʿaẓīm, 'a great punishment' (2:7), ʿadhābun alīm, 'a painful punishment' (2:10), and ʿadhābun muhīn, 'a humiliating punishment' (2:90).

primaryMeaning: To work or do something with intent and effort. Al-Rāghib notes that ʿamal is narrower than fiʿl, 'doing': it refers to acts done with purpose.
quranUsage: Occurs 360 times, above all in the pairing of faith with action: alladhīna āmanū wa ʿamilū al-ṣāliḥāt, 'those who believe and do righteous deeds' (first at 2:25). Nothing done is lost: 'Allah is not unaware of what you do (taʿmalūn)' (2:74), and 'whoever does (yaʿmal) an atom's weight of good will see it' (99:7).

primaryMeaning: To make, place or appoint — to put something into a state or a role. Unlike khalaqa, 'to create', jaʿala usually means making an existing thing into something or giving it a function.
quranUsage: Occurs 346 times, often describing how Allah shaped the world for people: 'who made (jaʿala) the earth a resting place for you and the sky a canopy' (2:22). It also describes appointing someone to a role: 'I will make you (jāʿiluka) a leader for mankind' (2:124), and 'I will place (jāʿilun) a successor on earth' (2:30).

primaryMeaning: Mercy and tender compassion. The root also gives raḥim, 'womb', and arḥām, 'ties of kinship'. In a ḥadīth qudsī, Allah says He named the womb (raḥim) from His own name, al-Raḥmān.
extendedMeaning: Arḥām, 'wombs' or 'ties of kinship', are named alongside Allah in 4:1: 'fear Allah, through whom you ask of one another, and the wombs (al-arḥām)'.
quranUsage: Occurs 339 times. Al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm, 'the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful', begin every Basmala (1:1). Classical scholars explain al-Raḥmān as mercy vast enough to embrace all creation — 'My mercy encompasses all things' (7:156) — and al-Raḥīm as mercy that continues and reaches the believers: 'He is ever merciful (raḥīman) to the believers' (33:43).

primaryMeaning: To be at ease with someone, familiar and sociable — the opposite of wildness or estrangement. Ins and insān, 'humankind', are usually linked to this root, since humans live in each other's company; some early scholars instead linked insān to nasiya, 'to forget'.
extendedMeaning: A second sense is to perceive something that brings comfort: Musa said, 'I have perceived (ānastu) a fire' (20:10).
quranUsage: Occurs 338 times, mostly as al-nās, 'people' or 'mankind', including the address yā ayyuhā al-nās, 'O mankind' (2:21), and as al-insān, 'man', often describing human nature: 'man was created weak' (4:28). Al-ins, 'humans', is paired with al-jinn: 'I did not create jinn and humans (al-ins) except to worship Me' (51:56).

primaryMeaning: To see — with the eyes, and by extension with the mind. Ra'y is an opinion, a view one 'sees'; ru'yā is a dream or vision.
quranUsage: Occurs 328 times. Often it is a question inviting reflection, a-lam tara, 'Have you not seen?', meaning 'have you not considered?' even about events the listener never witnessed: 'Have you not seen how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant?' (105:1). Ru'yā is used for dreams that carry meaning, such as Yusuf's and the king's (12:5, 12:43).

primaryMeaning: To write — and originally, according to Ibn Fāris, to bring one thing together with another, as writing joins letters into words; a katība is a body of troops gathered together. Because what is written is fixed, kataba also means to prescribe or decree.
quranUsage: Occurs 319 times, most often as al-kitāb, 'the Book': for the Quran — 'This is the Book about which there is no doubt' (2:2) — and for earlier scripture, as in ahl al-kitāb, 'People of the Book' (3:64). Kutiba, 'it has been prescribed', introduces obligations: 'Fasting has been prescribed for you' (2:183).

primaryMeaning: To guide someone on their way with gentleness. Al-Rāghib defines hidāya as 'guidance given with kindness'; from the same root comes hadiyya, 'gift', something sent kindly to another, and hady, animals sent as an offering to the Kaaba (2:196).
quranUsage: Occurs 316 times. Hudā, 'guidance', describes the Quran from its opening: 'guidance for the God-conscious (hudan lil-muttaqīn)' (2:2). The prayer ihdinā al-ṣirāṭ al-mustaqīm, 'Guide us to the straight path' (1:6), is recited in every unit of prayer. The Quran separates showing the way from opening the heart to it: 'You do not guide whom you love, but Allah guides whom He wills' (28:56).

primaryMeaning: Ibn Fāris gives this root two senses: darkness (ẓulma), the opposite of light, and putting something where it does not belong, overstepping its limit. Ẓulm, 'wrongdoing' or 'injustice', is the second: treating something other than as it deserves.
extendedMeaning: Ẓulumāt, 'darknesses', is set against light: Allah brings the believers 'out of the darknesses into the light' (2:257).
quranUsage: Occurs 315 times, mostly for wrongdoing: al-ẓālimūn, 'the wrongdoers' (first at 2:35). The Quran stresses that wrongdoers harm themselves: 'they did not wrong Us, but they were wronging themselves (anfusahum yaẓlimūn)' (2:57). Luqman calls shirk 'a tremendous wrong (ẓulmun ʿaẓīm)' (31:13).

primaryMeaning: The self or soul. Classical lexicographers connect nafs with nafas, 'breath', and with nafīs, 'precious' — the self being what a person holds most dear.
quranUsage: Occurs 298 times, often meaning 'oneself' (anfusahum, 'themselves') or 'a soul', a person: 'Every soul (nafs) will taste death' (3:185). The Quran describes states of the soul: 'the soul that commands to evil (ammāratun bil-sū')' (12:53), 'the self-reproaching soul (al-nafs al-lawwāma)' (75:2), and 'the soul at peace (al-nafs al-muṭma'inna)' (89:27).

primaryMeaning: To face something, to be in front of it. Ibn Fāris says every word of this root goes back to one thing facing another. From facing comes qabl, 'before' — what lies ahead in time — and qabila, 'to accept', to receive something face to face. Qibla is the direction one faces.
quranUsage: Occurs 294 times, mostly as qabl, 'before', especially for earlier peoples and scriptures: 'what was sent down before you (min qablika)' (2:4). Qibla, the direction of prayer, is the subject of 2:142–150: 'We will turn you to a qibla (qiblatan) that pleases you' (2:144). Ibrahim and Ismail prayed, 'Our Lord, accept (taqabbal) from us' (2:127).

primaryMeaning: To come down from a height, and to stop and stay somewhere — a traveller 'descends' on a place to lodge. Manzil is a lodging, and nuzul is the welcome prepared for an arriving guest.
extendedMeaning: Nuzul, 'welcome' or 'hospitality', describes Paradise: 'the Gardens of Firdaws will be their welcome (nuzulā)' (18:107).
quranUsage: Occurs 293 times, above all for revelation: anzala and nazzala, 'He sent down', describe the Quran coming from Allah — 'We sent it down (anzalnāhu) on the Night of Decree' (97:1). Some classical scholars note that nazzala suggests sending down in stages, and anzala all at once. Rain is also 'sent down' from the sky (2:22).

primaryMeaning: To remember and to mention — to bring something to mind or onto the tongue. Dhikr covers both the inner act of remembering and the outward act of speaking of it. The same root gives dhakar, 'male'.
extendedMeaning: Dhakar, 'male', is paired with unthā, 'female': 'We created you from a male (dhakarin) and a female' (49:13).
quranUsage: Occurs 292 times. Remembering Allah is urged throughout: 'Remember Me (fa-dhkurūnī); I will remember you' (2:152), and 'in the remembrance of Allah (bi-dhikri Allāh) hearts find rest' (13:28). The Quran calls itself al-dhikr, 'the Reminder': 'We sent down the Reminder, and We will guard it' (15:9). La'allakum tadhakkarūn, 'so that you may take heed', closes many verses (6:152).

primaryMeaning: To be firm, established and true; Ibn Fāris says the root points to firmness and soundness. Ḥaqq is what really is — truth, reality — and also what is rightly due to someone.
extendedMeaning: Al-Ḥāqqa, 'the Inevitable Reality', is a name of the Day of Judgment and the title of Surah 69 (69:1). Ḥaqq also means a due or duty, as in 'a duty (ḥaqqan) on the God-conscious' (2:180).
quranUsage: Occurs 287 times, often as al-ḥaqq, 'the truth', set against bāṭil, falsehood: 'Truth has come and falsehood has vanished' (17:81). Bil-ḥaqq, 'in truth' or 'with purpose', describes how Allah created the heavens and the earth (6:73) and sent down the Book (2:176). Al-Ḥaqq, 'the Truth', is a name of Allah (22:6).

primaryMeaning: To lie — to say what does not match reality. The intensive form kadhdhaba means to call someone a liar, and so to deny or reject what they bring.
extendedMeaning: 'Inventing a lie (kadhiban) against Allah' is named among the gravest wrongs (6:21).
quranUsage: Occurs 282 times, mostly for denying Allah's signs and messengers: kadhdhabū, 'they denied' (3:11). Surah Al-Raḥmān asks 31 times, 'So which of the favours of your Lord will you both deny (tukadhdhibān)?' (55:13), and Surah Al-Mursalāt repeats, 'Woe that Day to the deniers (lil-mukadhdhibīn)' (77:15).

primaryMeaning: To come or arrive; jā'a bi- ('to come with') means to bring. Al-Rāghib notes that it is more general than atā, which suggests coming with ease.
quranUsage: Occurs 278 times, often for the arrival of truth, messengers and signs: 'when there came to them (jā'ahum) a Messenger from Allah' (2:101), 'Truth has come (jā'a al-ḥaqq)' (17:81), and 'When the help of Allah comes (jā'a), and the victory' (110:1).

primaryMeaning: To serve and humble oneself. Ibn Fāris notes the root joins gentleness with lowliness: a road smoothed by many feet was called ṭarīq muʿabbad. ʿAbd is a servant, and ʿibāda, 'worship', is complete humble service.
extendedMeaning: The Prophet is honoured with the title 'His servant (ʿabdihi)' in the account of the Night Journey (17:1).
quranUsage: Occurs 275 times. Worship is the purpose of creation: 'I did not create jinn and humans except to worship Me (li-yaʿbudūn)' (51:56), and every prayer contains iyyāka naʿbudu, 'You alone we worship' (1:5). Allah often calls people 'My servants (ʿibādī)' with closeness: 'When My servants ask you about Me, I am near' (2:186).

primaryMeaning: To take or take hold of — from simply taking something in hand to seizing it firmly. The form ittakhadha means to take something up as one's own: to adopt it, or to treat it as something.
extendedMeaning: Yahya is told, 'Take (khudh) the Book with strength' (19:12).
quranUsage: Occurs 273 times. Ittakhadha often describes taking false gods or claiming a son for Allah: 'They say, "Allah has taken a son (ittakhadha)"' (2:116). 'We took your covenant (akhadhnā mīthāqakum)' recalls binding pledges (2:63). It is also used for Allah seizing wrongdoers: 'Allah seized them (fa-akhadhahum) for their sins' (3:11).

primaryMeaning: To measure out and shape. Ibn Fāris gives two senses: determining the measure of a thing, and smoothness. Creating is bringing something into being according to a set measure. Khuluq, 'character', is a person's inner shape.
extendedMeaning: Of the Prophet: 'And you are truly of a great character (khuluqin ʿaẓīm)' (68:4).
quranUsage: Occurs 261 times, mostly for Allah's creating: 'who created (khalaqa) the heavens and the earth' (6:1). The Quran points to creation as evidence of resurrection: 'Is not He who created the heavens and the earth able to create (yakhluqa) the like of them?' (36:81). Al-Khāliq, 'the Creator', is a name of Allah (59:24).

primaryMeaning: To guard or shield something from harm. Wiqāya is protection, and taqwā is guarding oneself — keeping a shield between oneself and what one fears, above all Allah's displeasure.
extendedMeaning: 'Protect (qū) yourselves and your families from a Fire' (66:6).
quranUsage: Occurs 258 times, mostly as ittaqū, 'be mindful of' or 'fear' (Allah), and al-muttaqūn, 'the God-conscious', for whom the Quran is guidance (2:2). 'The most noble of you with Allah is the most God-conscious (atqākum)' (49:13). The prayer 'protect us (qinā) from the punishment of the Fire' uses the plain sense (2:201).

primaryMeaning: To be behind, to come later. Ākhir is 'last', what comes at the end; ākhar is 'another', a second thing that follows the first; and akhkhara is 'to delay', to put something back.
quranUsage: Occurs 250 times, most often as al-ākhira, 'the Hereafter' — the life that comes after this one, contrasted with al-dunyā, 'the near life': 'the Hereafter is better and more lasting' (87:17). Belief in al-yawm al-ākhir, 'the Last Day', is paired with belief in Allah (2:8). Al-Ākhir, 'the Last', is a name of Allah (57:3).

primaryMeaning: To command — and also an affair or matter, the thing one is concerned with. Amīr, 'commander', and umūr, 'affairs', both come from it.
extendedMeaning: Ulū al-amr, 'those in authority', are to be obeyed after Allah and His Messenger (4:59).
quranUsage: Occurs 248 times. Amr is Allah's command — 'His command (amruhu), when He wills a thing, is only to say to it "Be", and it is' (36:82) — and affairs in general: 'to Allah all matters (al-umūr) are returned' (2:210). Believers are those who 'enjoin what is right (ya'murūna bil-maʿrūf)' (3:104).

primaryMeaning: To be far away. From distance in space comes baʿd, 'after' — what is distant in time.
quranUsage: Occurs 235 times, mostly as baʿd, 'after': 'after the clear proofs had come to them (min baʿdi)' (3:105). Baʿīd, 'far', describes deep error — 'straying far away (ḍalālan baʿīdā)' (4:60). Buʿdan, 'away with…', is said of the drowned people of Nuh (11:44).

primaryMeaning: To cover and shield. A mighfar is a helmet, which covers and protects the head; maghfira, 'forgiveness', is Allah covering a sin and shielding the sinner from its consequences.
extendedMeaning: Nuh told his people, 'Ask forgiveness of your Lord (istaghfirū); He is ever forgiving' (71:10).
quranUsage: Occurs 234 times, most often describing Allah as ghafūr, 'Oft-Forgiving' (about 90 times), usually paired with raḥīm, 'Merciful' (2:173). He is also al-Ghaffār, 'the Ever-Forgiving': 'I am ever-forgiving (la-ghaffārun) to whoever repents' (20:82). 'Allah forgives all sins (yaghfiru al-dhunūba jamīʿā)' for those who return to Him (39:53).

primaryMeaning: To be next to, to follow closely with nothing in between; Ibn Fāris says the root means nearness. A walī is one who is close — a friend, ally, protector or guardian. The same root gives tawallā, 'to turn away', literally to turn one's back.
extendedMeaning: Mawlā, 'patron' or 'protector', ends Al-Baqarah: 'You are our Protector (mawlānā)' (2:286). Awlā means 'closer' or 'more entitled': 'The Prophet is closer (awlā) to the believers than their own selves' (33:6).
quranUsage: Occurs 232 times. 'Allah is the protector (walī) of those who believe' (2:257), and believers are warned against taking the wrong allies (awliyā') (3:28). Tawallaw, 'they turned away', describes rejecting the message (2:137).

primaryMeaning: To call someone, to invite them towards you. Duʿā' is calling on Allah in prayer, and daʿwa is inviting others.
quranUsage: Occurs 212 times. It is used for prayer: 'Call on Me (udʿūnī); I will answer you' (40:60), and 'I answer the call of the caller when he calls on Me (daʿāni)' (2:186). It also describes calling on false gods — 'those you call on (tadʿūna) besides Allah are servants like you' (7:194) — and inviting others: 'Invite (udʿu) to the way of your Lord with wisdom' (16:125).

primaryMeaning: To restrain; Ibn Fāris says the root's one meaning is holding back, like the ḥakama, the bit that restrains a horse. Ḥukm, 'judgment', holds back injustice, and ḥikma, 'wisdom', holds a person back from foolishness.
extendedMeaning: Muḥkamāt, 'precise verses', are the clear foundation of the Book, set beside verses open to more than one meaning (3:7).
quranUsage: Occurs 210 times. Ḥakīm, 'All-Wise', describes Allah, often paired with ʿAzīz, 'Almighty', or ʿAlīm, 'All-Knowing' (2:32). The Prophet 'teaches them the Book and wisdom (al-ḥikma)' (2:129). Yaḥkumu, 'He judges', is used for Allah deciding between people on the Day of Resurrection (2:113).

primaryMeaning: To own and have control, firmly and with power. Mulk is dominion, milk is possession, and malik is a king. This root is also usually given for malak, 'angel', though many scholars derive it instead from a-l-k, 'to carry a message'.
extendedMeaning: Mā malakat aymānukum, 'those your right hands possess', refers to people held in bondage (4:3).
quranUsage: Occurs 206 times. Dominion belongs to Allah: 'To Allah belongs the dominion (mulku) of the heavens and the earth' (2:107), and Al-Fātiḥah calls Him 'Master (māliki) of the Day of Judgment' (1:4). Al-malā'ika, 'the angels', accounts for about 70 occurrences: 'when your Lord said to the angels' (2:30).

primaryMeaning: To cover and conceal; Ibn Fāris says the root's one meaning is covering. The jinn are beings hidden from sight, a janna is a garden so thick with trees that the ground is hidden, a janīn is a child hidden in the womb, and junūn, 'madness', is reason being covered.
extendedMeaning: Junna, 'a shield', is what hides and protects: the hypocrites 'take their oaths as a cover (junnatan)' (58:16).
quranUsage: Occurs 201 times, mostly as janna and jannāt, 'Garden' and 'Gardens' — Paradise (about 150 times): 'Gardens beneath which rivers flow' (2:25). The jinn were created 'from a smokeless flame of fire' (55:15), and majnūn, 'possessed' or 'mad', is the charge thrown at the prophets (15:6).

primaryMeaning: ʿInda means 'at', 'with' or 'in the presence of' — being near someone or in their keeping. The same root gives ʿanīd, 'stubborn', one who stands apart and refuses.
extendedMeaning: ʿAnīd describes one who persists in rejecting the truth (50:24).
quranUsage: Occurs 201 times, mostly as ʿinda. ʿInda Allāh, 'with Allah', means what He holds or how things stand in His sight: 'What is with you runs out, and what is with Allah (ʿinda Allāh) remains' (16:96), and 'the religion with Allah is Islam' (3:19). The martyrs are 'alive with their Lord (ʿinda rabbihim)' (3:169).

primaryMeaning: Good, and what is better. Ibn Fāris says the root rests on inclination: khayr is what people are drawn to, and ikhtiyār, 'choosing', is taking the better of two things.
extendedMeaning: 'Your Lord creates what He wills and chooses (yakhtāru)' (28:68).
quranUsage: Occurs 196 times, often as khayr, 'better', comparing this life with the next: 'the Hereafter is better (khayrun) for you than the first' (93:4). Khayr is also wealth and every good thing — 'whatever good (khayrin) you spend' (2:215) — and believers are told to 'race towards good things (al-khayrāt)' (2:148).

primaryMeaning: Beauty and goodness together: ḥusn is anything pleasing, in appearance, action or character. Iḥsān is doing something well and doing good to others; in the ḥadīth of Jibrīl it is 'to worship Allah as if you see Him'.
extendedMeaning: 'Is the reward for good (al-iḥsān) anything but good?' (55:60).
quranUsage: Occurs 194 times. 'Allah loves those who do good (al-muḥsinīn)' (2:195). Ḥasana, 'a good thing' or 'a good deed', appears in the prayer 'give us good (ḥasanatan) in this world and good in the Hereafter' (2:201). Al-asmā' al-ḥusnā, 'the most beautiful names', belong to Allah (7:180).

primaryMeaning: Light. Nūr is light that illuminates, and nār, 'fire', belongs to the same root as a source of light and heat.
extendedMeaning: The Quran is called 'a clear light (nūran mubīnā)' (4:174), and the Prophet 'a light-giving lamp (sirājan munīrā)' (33:46).
quranUsage: Occurs 194 times; about 145 of these are al-nār, 'the Fire': 'fear the Fire whose fuel is people and stones' (2:24). Nūr, 'light', is used for guidance and for Allah Himself: 'Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth' (24:35), and He brings believers 'out of the darknesses into the light (al-nūr)' (2:257).

primaryMeaning: To lose the way, to go astray — and also to be lost or vanish from sight. Ḍalāl is being off the right path, whether through ignorance or deliberately.
extendedMeaning: The sense of 'being lost' appears in 6:24: 'what they used to invent has left them (ḍalla ʿanhum)'. Musa says of his past, 'I did it then when I was of those astray (al-ḍāllīn)' — that is, not yet guided (26:20).
quranUsage: Occurs 191 times. Al-ḍāllīn, 'those who have gone astray', closes Al-Fātiḥah (1:7). Ḍalālun mubīn, 'clear error', describes being lost without guidance (3:164). Yuḍillu, 'He leaves to stray', is used of Allah letting astray those who choose it: 'He leaves none to stray by it except the defiantly disobedient' (2:26).

primaryMeaning: To live. Ḥayāt is life, and ḥayā', 'modesty' or 'shyness', comes from the same root — classically explained as a living heart shrinking from what is shameful.
extendedMeaning: Rain 'gives life to the earth after its death' (2:164), and the Hereafter is 'the true life (la-hiya al-ḥayawān)' (29:64).
quranUsage: Occurs 189 times. Al-ḥayāt al-dunyā, 'the life of this world', is often contrasted with the Hereafter (2:85). 'My Lord is He who gives life (yuḥyī) and causes death' (2:258). Al-Ḥayy, 'the Ever-Living', is a name of Allah (2:255).

primaryMeaning: To hear. Samʿ is both the sense of hearing and the act of listening, and it often implies heeding what is heard.
extendedMeaning: Hearing is named first among the faculties a person will be questioned about: 'the hearing, the sight and the heart' (17:36).
quranUsage: Occurs 185 times. Samīʿ, 'All-Hearing', describes Allah, usually paired with ʿAlīm, 'All-Knowing' (2:127). The believers' answer to revelation is samiʿnā wa aṭaʿnā, 'we hear and we obey' (2:285), while others said, 'we hear and we disobey' (2:93).

primaryMeaning: To build — Ibn Fāris says the root means joining one part of a thing to another. Grammarians also place ibn, 'son', and banūn, 'sons', here.
extendedMeaning: Nuh called to his son, yā bunayya, 'O my dear son', to board the ship with them (11:42).
quranUsage: Occurs 184 times, mostly as banī, 'children' or 'descendants', in banī isrā'īl, 'the Children of Israel' (2:40), and ibn, 'son', as in ʿĪsā ibn Maryam, 'Isa son of Maryam' (2:87). Binā', 'a structure', describes the sky: 'and the sky a canopy (binā'an)' (2:22).

primaryMeaning: To go out, to emerge. Akhraja is to bring or drive something out, and kharāj, 'revenue' or 'tribute', is what comes out of the land or is paid out.
quranUsage: Occurs 182 times. Allah brings forth life: 'He brings the living out (yukhriju) of the dead' (6:95), and 'We bring forth (fa-akhrajnā) with it plants of every kind' (6:99). It describes being driven out, as Satan 'drove your parents out (akhraja) of the Garden' (7:27), and the resurrection, 'the Day of coming out (yawm al-khurūj)' (50:42).

primaryMeaning: To be sound and right — the opposite of fasād, 'corruption'. Ṣāliḥ is what is sound and fitting, iṣlāḥ is setting something right, and ṣulḥ is reconciliation between people.
quranUsage: Occurs 180 times, most often in 'those who believe and do righteous deeds (al-ṣāliḥāt)' (2:25). Al-ṣāliḥūn, 'the righteous', is a rank of prophets and believers: Ibrahim 'in the Hereafter will be among the righteous' (2:130). Aṣlaḥa, 'to make amends', follows repentance: 'except those who repent and make amends (aṣlaḥū)' (2:160).

primaryMeaning: A way or road, especially one that is open and easy to travel; by extension, any means of reaching something. Ibn al-sabīl, 'son of the road', is a traveller.
quranUsage: Occurs 176 times, most often in fī sabīli Allāh, 'in the way of Allah', for striving, spending and fighting in His cause (2:154, 2:261). Sabīl also means a means or a way through: Hajj is due on 'whoever is able to find a way (sabīlan) to it' (3:97). Ibn al-sabīl, 'the wayfarer', is named among those owed charity (2:177).

primaryMeaning: To follow — to walk behind someone, and by extension to go after, pursue, or take someone as one's lead. Tābiʿ is a follower.
extendedMeaning: Believers are to follow 'the way of Ibrahim, the upright (millata ibrāhīma ḥanīfā)' (4:125).
quranUsage: Occurs 172 times. It warns against following the wrong lead — 'do not follow (lā tattabiʿū) the footsteps of Satan' (2:168) — and calls to follow revelation: 'follow (ittabiʿū) what Allah has sent down' (2:170), and 'follow me (fa-ttabiʿūnī); Allah will love you' (3:31).

primaryMeaning: To kill. The form qātala means to fight — literally, to try to kill one another — so qitāl is fighting or combat.
extendedMeaning: 'Do not think of those killed (qutilū) in the way of Allah as dead; they are alive with their Lord' (3:169).
quranUsage: Occurs 170 times. It forbids killing — 'do not kill yourselves (lā taqtulū anfusakum)' (4:29), and 'whoever kills a soul … it is as if he had killed all mankind' (5:32) — and sets the limits of fighting: 'Fight in the way of Allah those who fight you (yuqātilūnakum), but do not transgress' (2:190).

primaryMeaning: To be like something, to stand in its place. Mithl is 'a like' or equal; mathal is a likeness — a parable, example or description that sets one thing beside another so it can be understood.
quranUsage: Occurs 169 times. Allah 'strikes parables (al-amthāl) for people so that they may reflect' (59:21), from the gnat (2:26) to the light in a niche (24:35). Mithl appears in the challenge to produce 'a surah like it (min mithlihi)' (2:23) and in 'There is nothing like Him (ka-mithlihi)' (42:11).

primaryMeaning: To share, to have a part in something together with another. Sharīk is a partner; shirk is ascribing partners to Allah — giving another a share in what belongs to Him alone.
extendedMeaning: In the inheritance rulings, shurakā' keeps its everyday meaning of 'sharers' (4:12).
quranUsage: Occurs 168 times. Al-mushrikūn, 'those who associate partners with Allah', are named alongside the People of the Book (2:105). 'Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him (an yushraka bihi), but forgives what is less than that for whom He wills' (4:48). Shurakā', 'partners', are the false gods people claimed (6:100).

primaryMeaning: To turn something over, to flip it. The heart (qalb) is named from this root for its constant turning; the Prophet would pray, 'O Turner of hearts (muqallib al-qulūb), make my heart firm on Your religion'.
extendedMeaning: Inqalaba, 'to turn back': 'will you turn back on your heels (inqalabtum)?' (3:144).
quranUsage: Occurs 168 times, mostly as qulūb, 'hearts' — in the Quran the seat of understanding and faith: 'Allah has set a seal on their hearts (qulūbihim)' (2:7), 'in their hearts is a disease' (2:10), and on the Day of Judgment only 'one who comes to Allah with a sound heart (bi-qalbin salīm)' will benefit (26:89).

primaryMeaning: What is bad, harmful or displeasing. Sū' is evil or harm, sayyi'a is a bad deed, and saw'a — what is shameful to uncover — is used for nakedness.
extendedMeaning: Saw'āt, 'nakedness', became visible to Adam and his wife when they tasted the tree (7:22).
quranUsage: Occurs 167 times. Sayyi'āt, 'evil deeds', are set against good ones: 'good deeds remove evil deeds (al-sayyi'āt)' (11:114). Sū' al-ʿadhāb, 'the worst of torment', describes Pharaoh's oppression of the Israelites (2:49). Sā'a, 'how evil!', condemns a deed: 'evil (sā'a) is what they do' (5:66).

primaryMeaning: To be many or much — the opposite of qilla, 'being few'. Kathīr is 'many', akthar is 'most', and kawthar is a great abundance.
extendedMeaning: Takāthur, 'competing for more', is the distraction condemned in 102:1.
quranUsage: Occurs 167 times, often for the majority: 'most of them (aktharuhum) do not believe' (2:100), 'most people are not grateful' (2:243). Believers are told to remember Allah 'much (dhikran kathīrā)' (33:41). Al-Kawthar, 'abundance', is given to the Prophet (108:1).

primaryMeaning: To die; the root is the opposite of life. It is also used for stillness: dead land is land without growth, and a heart without understanding is described as dead.
extendedMeaning: Death is part of the test: 'who created death and life to test you, which of you is best in deeds' (67:2).
quranUsage: Occurs 165 times. 'Every soul will taste death (al-mawt)' (3:185). Allah 'gives life and causes death (yumītu)' (2:258), and rain revives the land 'after its death (mawtihā)' (2:164). The dead (al-mawtā) will be raised: 'He gives life to the dead' (22:6).

primaryMeaning: To be great or large — in size, age or importance. Kibr and istikbār are claiming greatness for oneself, arrogance. Takbīr is declaring Allah great: Allāhu akbar.
extendedMeaning: Kabā'ir, 'major sins': 'if you avoid the major sins you are forbidden, We will remove your lesser misdeeds' (4:31).
quranUsage: Occurs 161 times. Akbar, 'greater', ranks things: 'the pleasure of Allah is greater (akbar)' (9:72). Istakbara, 'to be arrogant', describes refusing the truth: Iblis 'refused and was arrogant (istakbara)' (2:34). Al-Kabīr, 'the Most Great', and al-Mutakabbir, 'the Supreme', are names of Allah (13:9, 59:23).

primaryMeaning: To be present and see with one's own eyes. From presence comes testimony: a shāhid, 'witness', reports what he was present for. Al-shahāda is also 'the seen world', as opposed to al-ghayb, 'the unseen'.
extendedMeaning: Shahīd also means one who dies in Allah's way. The shuhadā' are named with the prophets, the truthful and the righteous (4:69).
quranUsage: Occurs 160 times. The believers are 'witnesses (shuhadā') over mankind, and the Messenger a witness over you' (2:143). Allah is 'Knower of the unseen and the seen (al-shahāda)' (6:73). The rules for witnessing a debt are set out in 2:282.

primaryMeaning: Naba' is news of great importance. A nabī, 'prophet', is classically explained as one who receives news from Allah and brings it to people; some derive it instead from nabwa, 'raised ground', a prophet being raised in rank.
quranUsage: Occurs 160 times, mostly as al-nabī, 'the Prophet', and al-nabiyyūn, 'the prophets' (2:61). Naba' is weighty news: 'About the great news (al-naba' al-ʿaẓīm)' (78:2). Yunabbi'ukum, 'He will inform you', describes Allah telling people what they did (5:48).

primaryMeaning: A part or portion of something. Baʿḍ means 'some'; baʿḍuhum baʿḍan, 'some of them … others', expresses what people do to one another. The same root gives baʿūḍa, 'gnat', a tiny creature.
quranUsage: Occurs 158 times, almost always as baʿḍ, 'some' or 'part': 'Do you believe in part (bi-baʿḍi) of the Book and disbelieve in part?' (2:85). It describes relations between people: 'the believing men and women are allies of one another (baʿḍuhum awliyā'u baʿḍ)' (9:71). 'Allah is not shy to set forth the example of a gnat (baʿūḍatan)' (2:26).

primaryMeaning: To help and support someone against an opponent, and so to give victory. Naṣīr and nāṣir mean 'helper'. Al-naṣārā, 'the Christians', is traditionally linked to this root — through the town of Nazareth (al-Nāṣira), or to the disciples' answer, 'We are the helpers (anṣār) of Allah' (3:52).
quranUsage: Occurs 158 times. Victory comes from Allah: 'victory (al-naṣr) is only from Allah' (3:126), and 'When the help of Allah (naṣru Allāh) comes, and the victory' (110:1). 'If you support Allah, He will support you (yanṣurkum)' (47:7). Naṣīr, 'Helper', describes Allah (4:45).

primaryMeaning: To be true — for words to match reality and for a person to be sincere. Ṣidq is truthfulness; ṣaddaqa is to confirm something as true; and ṣadaqa, 'charity', is classically explained as giving that proves the truth of one's faith.
extendedMeaning: Ṣiddīq, 'utterly truthful', describes Ibrahim and Idris (19:41, 19:56) and Maryam (5:75).
quranUsage: Occurs 155 times. Believers are told to 'be with the truthful (al-ṣādiqīn)' (9:119). Muṣaddiq, 'confirming', describes the Quran confirming the scripture before it (2:41). The rightful recipients of ṣadaqāt, 'charities', are named in 9:60.

primaryMeaning: To be other or different. Ghayr means 'other than' or 'not'; taghyīr is changing a thing into something else; and ghayra is protective jealousy — not tolerating another's claim on what is yours.
quranUsage: Occurs 154 times, mostly as ghayr: 'not (ghayri) of those who earned anger' (1:7), and 'you have no god other than Him (ghayruhu)' (7:59). Bi-ghayri al-ḥaqq, 'without right', describes unjust killing (2:61). 'Allah does not change (lā yughayyiru) the condition of a people until they change what is in themselves' (13:11).

primaryMeaning: To promise. Waʿd is usually a promise of good, while waʿīd is a threat of punishment. Mīʿād and mawʿid are the appointed time or place of what is promised.
quranUsage: Occurs 151 times. 'The promise of Allah (waʿda Allāh) is true' recurs throughout (4:122), and 'Allah does not break His promise (al-mīʿād)' (3:9). It is also used for Satan's false promises: 'Satan promises you (yaʿidukum) poverty' (2:268).

primaryMeaning: To see clearly. Baṣar is eyesight, and baṣīra is insight — seeing with the heart.
extendedMeaning: 'I call to Allah with clear insight (ʿalā baṣīratin)' (12:108).
quranUsage: Occurs 148 times. Baṣīr, 'All-Seeing', describes Allah, often in 'Allah sees what they do' (2:96). The real blindness is of the heart: 'It is not the eyes that go blind, but the hearts within the breasts' (22:46). 'Vision (al-abṣār) cannot reach Him, but He reaches all vision' (6:103).

primaryMeaning: To go back and forth seeking something, like a scout (rā'id) searching for pasture. Arāda, 'to want' or 'to intend', is to seek something with one's will; rāwada is to try persistently to persuade someone.
quranUsage: Occurs 148 times, mostly as yurīdu, 'He wills' or 'He intends': 'Allah intends ease for you and does not intend hardship' (2:185). 'His command, when He wills (arāda) a thing, is only to say "Be"' (36:82). Rāwadat describes the wife of al-ʿAzīz trying to seduce Yusuf (12:23).

primaryMeaning: To meet, to come face to face with something. Alqā, 'to throw' or 'to cast', is to make something meet a place; it is also used for delivering words to someone.
extendedMeaning: Adam 'received (fa-talaqqā) words from his Lord', and He accepted his repentance (2:37).
quranUsage: Occurs 146 times. Liqā', 'meeting', refers above all to meeting Allah: 'whoever hopes to meet his Lord (liqā'a rabbihi), let him do righteous work' (18:110). Alqā describes Pharaoh's magicians casting their ropes and staffs before Musa (7:116).

primaryMeaning: Below, or short of something. Dūna means 'beneath', 'other than' or 'besides' — whatever falls short of the thing it is compared with.
extendedMeaning: Dūna also means 'less than': Allah 'forgives what is less than that (mā dūna dhālika)' — less than shirk (4:48).
quranUsage: Occurs 144 times, mostly as min dūni Allāh, 'besides Allah' or 'other than Allah', for the false gods people call on (2:23). It stresses that there is no protector beside Him: 'you have no protector or helper besides Allah (min dūni Allāh)' (2:107).

primaryMeaning: To be sound, safe and whole. Salām is peace and safety; islām is surrendering oneself wholly to Allah; a muslim is one who surrenders.
extendedMeaning: On the Day of Judgment what benefits is 'a sound heart (qalbin salīm)' (26:89).
quranUsage: Occurs 140 times. 'When his Lord said to him, "Submit (aslim)", he said, "I have submitted (aslamtu) to the Lord of the worlds"' (2:131). Salām is the greeting of believers and of Paradise: 'Peace be upon you (salāmun ʿalaykum)' (6:54). Al-Salām, 'the Source of Peace', is a name of Allah (59:23).

primaryMeaning: Softness and ease of life. Niʿma is a blessing or favour, and naʿīm is bliss. Anʿām, 'grazing livestock', shares the root — among the chief blessings of desert life.
extendedMeaning: Niʿma, 'how excellent!', praises: 'an excellent (niʿma) Protector and an excellent Helper' (8:40).
quranUsage: Occurs 140 times. 'Remember the favour of Allah (niʿmata Allāh) upon you' (3:103); 'if you tried to count Allah's blessings, you could not number them' (14:34). Al-Fātiḥah asks for 'the path of those You have blessed (anʿamta ʿalayhim)' (1:7), and Paradise is jannāt al-naʿīm, 'Gardens of Bliss' (5:65).

primaryMeaning: To be near. Dunyā, 'this world', is literally 'the nearer' life, the one close at hand; adnā means 'nearer', 'lower' or 'lesser'.
extendedMeaning: Adnā can mean 'lower' in worth: 'Would you exchange what is better for what is lower (adnā)?' (2:61).
quranUsage: Occurs 133 times; 115 of these are al-dunyā, 'this world', usually in al-ḥayāt al-dunyā, 'the life of this world' (2:85): 'the life of this world is only the enjoyment of delusion' (3:185). The lowest heaven is al-samā' al-dunyā, 'the nearest sky', adorned with lamps (67:5).

primaryMeaning: To measure, and to have power over something. Qadar is the measure set for things — decree; qudra is power; and qadara ʿalā, 'to restrict', is to measure something out narrowly.
extendedMeaning: Qadr also means true worth: 'They did not esteem Allah as He deserves (ḥaqqa qadrihi)' (6:91).
quranUsage: Occurs 132 times. Qadīr, 'All-Powerful', ends many verses: 'Allah has power over all things' (2:20). 'We created everything in due measure (bi-qadarin)' (54:49). Laylat al-qadr, 'the Night of Decree', is 'better than a thousand months' (97:3). Allah extends provision or restricts it (yaqdiru) (13:26).

primaryMeaning: To warn of danger — to tell someone of something so they can guard against it. Nadhr, 'a vow', shares the root: a pledge one binds oneself to.
extendedMeaning: Nadhr, 'vow': Maryam said, 'I have vowed (nadhartu) a fast to the Most Merciful' (19:26).
quranUsage: Occurs 130 times. Nadhīr, 'warner', describes the prophets and the Prophet: 'he is only a clear warner (nadhīrun mubīn)' (7:184), sent 'as a bearer of good news and a warner (nadhīran)' (2:119). Surah Al-Qamar asks after each destroyed people, 'how were My punishment and My warnings (nudhuri)?' (54:16).

primaryMeaning: To gather, to bring together what was scattered. Jamīʿ means 'all together', jamʿ is a gathering or host, and jumuʿa, 'Friday', is the day of congregation.
extendedMeaning: Jamaʿa also means hoarding: 'who gathered (jamaʿa) wealth and counted it' (104:2).
quranUsage: Occurs 129 times, often as jamīʿan, 'all' or 'together': 'hold fast to the rope of Allah, all together (jamīʿan)' (3:103). Yawm al-jamʿ, 'the Day of Gathering', is the Day of Judgment (64:9). The Friday prayer is commanded in 62:9: 'when the call is made for prayer on the day of Jumuʿa'.

primaryMeaning: To ask — to question, or to request something. Su'āl is a question, and sā'il is one who asks, including one who asks for help.
extendedMeaning: 'As for the one who asks (al-sā'il), do not turn him away' (93:10).
quranUsage: Occurs 129 times. Yas'alūnaka, 'they ask you', introduces answers to questions put to the Prophet — about the new moons, about wine and gambling (2:189, 2:219). 'You will surely be asked (la-tus'alunna) about what you used to do' (16:93). The Prophet is told to say, 'I do not ask you (as'alukum) for any payment for it' (6:90).

primaryMeaning: To comply willingly, to be obedient. Ṭāʿa is obedience given freely; istaṭāʿa, 'to be able', is to find something within one's power — something that yields to you.
extendedMeaning: The heavens and the earth answered Allah, 'We come willingly (ṭā'iʿīn)' (41:11).
quranUsage: Occurs 129 times. 'Obey Allah and obey the Messenger (aṭīʿū)' recurs throughout (4:59). Istaṭāʿa sets the limit of duty: Hajj is due on 'whoever is able (istaṭāʿa) to find a way to it' (3:97), and 'fear Allah as much as you are able (istaṭaʿtum)' (64:16).

primaryMeaning: To look at something carefully, to examine it. From looking comes waiting — looking out for what will come — and naẓira, granting someone time.
extendedMeaning: On the Day of Judgment, 'faces that day will be radiant, looking (nāẓira) at their Lord' (75:23).
quranUsage: Occurs 129 times. Unẓur and unẓurū, 'look!', invite reflection: 'travel through the land and see (fa-nẓurū) how was the end of the deniers' (3:137), and 'Do they not look (yanẓurūna) at the camels, how they were created?' (88:17). Yanẓurūna also means 'they wait' (2:210), and yunẓarūn, 'they will be given respite', says the punishment will not be delayed (2:162).

primaryMeaning: To be great and large. Ibn Fāris ties the root to size and strength, and ʿaẓm, 'bone', belongs to it as the hard frame of the body.
extendedMeaning: ʿIẓām, 'bones', appears in the deniers' question, 'When we are bones (ʿiẓāman) and crumbled dust, will we really be raised?' (17:49), and in the stages of creation: 'We made the lump into bones' (23:14).
quranUsage: Occurs 128 times, mostly as ʿaẓīm, 'great', describing Allah — 'He is the Most High, the Most Great (al-ʿAẓīm)' (2:255) — His bounty (2:105), the Throne (9:129), and great punishment (2:7). The Prophet's character is called 'great' (68:4).

primaryMeaning: The people who belong to someone or something: a man's family, a town's inhabitants, a book's followers. From belonging comes ahl li-, 'worthy of' — those who belong to something by right.
extendedMeaning: Ahl al-bayt, 'people of the house', is used for the household of the Prophet (33:33) and for Ibrahim's household (11:73). Allah is 'worthy (ahlu) of being feared, and worthy of forgiving' (74:56).
quranUsage: Occurs 127 times. Ahl al-kitāb, 'the People of the Book', recurs throughout: 'Say, O People of the Book (yā ahla al-kitāb), come to a word common between us and you' (3:64). Ahl is also one's household, as in Nuh's plea for his son: 'my son is of my family (ahlī)' (11:45).

primaryMeaning: To come behind or after. Khalf is 'behind'; khalīfa is a successor who comes after another and takes his place; and ikhtalafa, 'to differ', is literally for people to go in different directions, each leaving the other behind.
extendedMeaning: Ikhtilāf also describes the variety in creation: 'the alternation (ikhtilāf) of night and day' (2:164), and 'the diversity of your languages and colours' (30:22).
quranUsage: Occurs 127 times. Ikhtalafa, 'to differ', describes the divisions among earlier communities: 'Allah will judge between them in what they used to differ over (yakhtalifūn)' (2:113). Khalīfa, 'successor', is the role given to man on earth (2:30). Allah 'does not break (lā yukhlifu) the promise' (3:9).

primaryMeaning: To enter, to go inside. Adkhala is to bring someone in, and madkhal is a way in or place of entry.
extendedMeaning: 'Enter (udkhulū) into Islam completely' (2:208). Yusuf told his family, 'Enter Egypt, if Allah wills, in safety' (12:99).
quranUsage: Occurs 126 times, often for entering Paradise: 'He will admit him (yudkhilhu) to Gardens beneath which rivers flow' (4:13), and 'enter (udkhulū) Paradise for what you used to do' (16:32). It also describes the Israelites told to 'enter the gate bowing humbly' (2:58).

primaryMeaning: Ibn Fāris gives two senses: to go back to a starting point, and the beginning of a thing. Awwal, 'first', is where things start; ta'wīl, 'interpretation', is taking something back to what it finally means. The corpus also places āl here — a man's people or household, those who go back to him.
extendedMeaning: Ta'wīl, the true meaning of a thing, is known to Allah (3:7); it also describes the interpretation of Yusuf's dreams (12:100).
quranUsage: Occurs 125 times. Al-awwalūn, 'the former peoples', often appears in the deniers' dismissal, 'tales of the former peoples (asāṭīr al-awwalīn)' (6:25). Āl describes a following: 'the people of Pharaoh (āli firʿawn)' (2:49). Al-Awwal, 'the First', is a name of Allah (57:3).

primaryMeaning: To fear — to expect something harmful. Khawf is fear of what may come, and takhwīf is making someone afraid.
extendedMeaning: Lā takhaf, 'do not fear', reassures Musa before Pharaoh's magicians (20:68) and Lut when the angels came to him (29:33).
quranUsage: Occurs 124 times. 'No fear (khawfun) will be upon them, nor will they grieve' is promised to those who follow guidance (2:38). Believers call on their Lord 'in fear and hope (khawfan wa ṭamaʿan)' (7:56). Fear of Allah is praised: 'for whoever fears (khāfa) standing before his Lord there are two gardens' (55:46).

primaryMeaning: The outer skin. Bashar, 'human being', is named for the visible skin, in contrast to creatures covered by hair or feathers. Bushrā, 'good news', is news that shows on the skin of the face — makes it glow.
extendedMeaning: Maryam asked, 'How will I have a child when no man (basharun) has touched me?' (3:47).
quranUsage: Occurs 123 times. Bashshir, 'give good news', is a frequent command: 'give good news (bashshir) to those who believe and do righteous deeds' (2:25). The prophets are 'bearers of good news and warners (mubashshirīn)' (2:213). Bashar, 'a human', stresses the Prophet's humanity: 'I am only a human (basharun) like you' (18:110).

primaryMeaning: Provision — anything given that one benefits from, whether food, wealth, knowledge or children. Rizq is what is provided, and al-Razzāq is the One who provides.
extendedMeaning: 'He provides for him from where he does not expect' is promised to those who fear Allah (65:3).
quranUsage: Occurs 123 times. The God-conscious 'spend from what We have provided them (razaqnāhum)' (2:3). Provision is in Allah's hands: 'Allah extends provision (al-rizq) for whom He wills and restricts it' (13:26). 'Allah is the Provider (al-Razzāq), the Possessor of strength' (51:58).

primaryMeaning: Strength, might, and being hard to overcome. Ibn Fāris says the root means strength and force. ʿIzz is honour and power; ʿazīz is one who cannot be defeated — and also what is rare and precious.
extendedMeaning: ʿIzza can also mean false pride: of the arrogant it is said, 'pride (al-ʿizza) takes hold of him in sin' (2:206). Al-ʿAzīz is the title of the Egyptian official in the story of Yusuf (12:30).
quranUsage: Occurs 120 times, mostly as al-ʿAzīz, 'the Almighty', a name of Allah usually paired with al-Ḥakīm, 'the All-Wise' (2:129). 'All honour (al-ʿizza) belongs to Allah' (4:139), and 'honour belongs to Allah, His Messenger and the believers' (63:8).

primaryMeaning: The hand — and by extension power, possession, favour and what one has done. Bayna yadayhi, 'between his hands', means 'in front of' or 'before' something.
extendedMeaning: 'The hand of Allah is over their hands' describes the pledge of the believers (48:10).
quranUsage: Occurs 120 times. Aydīhim, 'their hands', often stands for what people have done: 'because of what their hands (aydīhim) have sent ahead' (2:95). 'Between his hands' means 'before': the Quran confirms 'what was before it (bayna yadayhi)' (2:97). Allah's hand is spoken of with power: 'In His hand (bi-yadihi) is the dominion' (67:1).

primaryMeaning: To aim for, to head towards. Umm, 'mother', is the source one turns to; umma, 'community', is a people who share a common aim or way; imām is the one people follow, who goes before them.
extendedMeaning: Umm al-kitāb, 'the mother of the Book', is the foundation of scripture (3:7). Ummahāt, 'mothers': 'Allah brought you out of the wombs of your mothers (ummahātikum) knowing nothing' (16:78).
quranUsage: Occurs 118 times, mostly as umma: 'You are the best community (ummatin) brought forth for mankind' (3:110), and 'Every community (ummatin) has a messenger' (10:47). Imām, 'leader', is the role Allah gives Ibrahim (2:124).

primaryMeaning: To repay or requite — to give in return for what was done, whether good or bad. Jazā' is recompense; jizya is a tax paid in return for protection.
extendedMeaning: On the Day of Judgment 'no soul will avail (tajzī) another in anything' (2:48). Jizya is mentioned in 9:29.
quranUsage: Occurs 118 times. 'Thus do We reward (najzī) the doers of good' is a refrain (6:84). Recompense fits the deed: 'the recompense (jazā') of an evil deed is an evil like it' (42:40), and 'Is the reward for good anything but good?' (55:60). Allah will 'reward (li-yajziya) those who believed' with justice (10:4).

primaryMeaning: Father. Ab is a father, and ābā' are fathers or forefathers — the ancestors from whom people take their ways.
quranUsage: Occurs 117 times. Ābā'unā, 'our forefathers', often appears in the refusal to follow revelation: 'We will follow what we found our fathers (ābā'anā) upon' (2:170). Yā abati, 'O my father', is the tender address of Ibrahim to his father (19:42) and of Yusuf to his (12:4).

primaryMeaning: To open up and flow wide. Nahr is a river, a channel cut open for water; nahār, 'daytime', is the wide open light between dawn and sunset.
extendedMeaning: 'As for the one who asks, do not repel (tanhar) him' (93:10) — nahara is to drive away harshly.
quranUsage: Occurs 113 times. Al-anhār, 'rivers', describes Paradise: 'Gardens beneath which rivers flow (al-anhāru)' (2:25), including rivers of water, milk, wine and honey (47:15). Al-nahār, 'the day', is paired with al-layl, 'the night', as a sign: 'the alternation of night and day (al-nahāri)' (2:164).

primaryMeaning: To go out and run out. Infāq, 'spending', is letting wealth go out of one's hands. A nafaq is a tunnel with an exit, and the jerboa's burrow has a hidden second hole (nāfiqā'); from this comes nifāq, 'hypocrisy' — having a hidden way out of faith.
extendedMeaning: 'You will never attain righteousness until you spend (tunfiqū) from what you love' (3:92).
quranUsage: Occurs 111 times. Believers are those who 'spend (yunfiqūna) from what We have provided them' (2:3), and spending in Allah's way is like a grain that grows seven ears (2:261). Al-munāfiqūn, 'the hypocrites', are described at length, and Surah 63 is named after them (63:1).

primaryMeaning: To eat. Ukul is food or the fruit a tree yields, and akala is also used for consuming or using up something, such as wealth.
extendedMeaning: The tree of the parable 'gives its fruit (ukulahā) at all times' (14:25).
quranUsage: Occurs 109 times. Kulū, 'eat', permits the good things: 'eat (kulū) of the good things We have provided you' (2:57). 'Do not consume (lā ta'kulū) one another's wealth unjustly' (2:188). Those who 'consume (ya'kulūna) the property of orphans unjustly are only consuming fire into their bellies' (4:10).

primaryMeaning: To count and reckon. Ḥisāb is reckoning or account; ḥasb, 'sufficiency', is what is counted as enough; and ḥasiba, 'to think', is to reckon something in one's mind.
extendedMeaning: 'Does man think (a-yaḥsabu) that We will not gather his bones?' (75:3).
quranUsage: Occurs 109 times. Allah is 'swift in account (sarīʿ al-ḥisāb)' (2:202) and gives 'without measure (bi-ghayri ḥisāb)' (2:212). The believers said, ḥasbunā Allāhu wa niʿma al-wakīl, 'Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs' (3:173). Taḥsabanna, 'do not think', corrects false assumptions (3:169).

primaryMeaning: Payment in return for work — a wage or reward. Ista'jara is to hire someone; ujūr is also the bridal due paid to a wife.
extendedMeaning: One of Shuʿayb's daughters said of Musa, 'hire him (istajirhu); the best one you can hire is the strong, the trustworthy' (28:26).
quranUsage: Occurs 108 times, mostly as ajr, 'reward': 'they will have their reward (ajruhum) with their Lord' (2:62), and a reward that is 'great' or 'never cut off' (4:40). Nuh tells his people, 'I have asked you for no payment; my reward (ajriya) is only from Allah' (10:72). Ujūrahunna refers to wives' bridal dues (4:24).

primaryMeaning: To do or act — the most general word for any action. Fiʿl is a deed, and fāʿil the one who does it.
extendedMeaning: 'Why do you say what you do not do (lā tafʿalūn)?' (61:2).
quranUsage: Occurs 108 times. Allah 'does what He wills (yafʿalu mā yashā')' (3:40). People are warned about what they do: 'if you do not (lam tafʿalū) — and you will never do it — then fear the Fire' (2:24). Allah's command is 'always carried out (mafʿūlan)' (4:47).

primaryMeaning: To find, to come upon something. From finding comes wujūd, 'existence' — being found — and wajd, 'strong feeling', what one finds within oneself.
extendedMeaning: 'You will not find (lan tajida) any change in the way of Allah' (33:62).
quranUsage: Occurs 107 times. People cling to 'what we found (wajadnā) our fathers upon' (5:104). On the Day of Judgment 'every soul will find (tajidu) what it did of good present before it' (3:30). Addressing the Prophet: 'Did He not find you (yajidka) an orphan and give you shelter?' (93:6).

primaryMeaning: To run, and to go beyond a limit. ʿAdw is running; iʿtidā', ʿudwān and ʿadā' are overstepping bounds — transgression and aggression; ʿaduww, 'enemy', is one who goes against you.
extendedMeaning: The literal sense of running opens Surah 100: 'By the chargers (al-ʿādiyāt), panting' (100:1).
quranUsage: Occurs 106 times. Satan is 'a clear enemy (ʿaduwwun mubīn)' to man (2:168), and after the Fall Adam and Iblis were sent down 'as enemies to one another' (2:36). 'Do not transgress (lā taʿtadū); Allah does not love the transgressors (al-muʿtadīn)' (2:190).

primaryMeaning: To return, to go back to where one came from. Marjiʿ is the place of return, and rajʿ is going back.
extendedMeaning: 'O soul at peace, return (irjiʿī) to your Lord, well-pleased and pleasing' (89:28).
quranUsage: Occurs 104 times, often for the return to Allah: 'then to Him you will be returned (turjaʿūn)' (2:28), and the words of the patient in hardship, 'We belong to Allah and to Him we will return (rājiʿūn)' (2:156). 'To Me is your return (marjiʿukum)' (3:55).

primaryMeaning: To be more, to exceed. Faḍl is what goes beyond what is due — surplus, and so bounty and grace; faḍḍala is to favour one over another.
extendedMeaning: Seeking bounty also means lawful trade: 'there is no blame on you for seeking bounty (faḍlan) from your Lord' during Hajj (2:198).
quranUsage: Occurs 104 times, mostly for Allah's bounty: 'Allah is the possessor of great bounty (al-faḍl al-ʿaẓīm)' (2:105), and 'Were it not for the grace (faḍlu) of Allah upon you' (2:64). Faḍḍala describes preference: 'those messengers — We favoured some of them over others' (2:253).

primaryMeaning: To hold back and restrain. Ṣabr, 'patience', is holding oneself firm — restraining the self from panic, the tongue from complaint, and the limbs from wrongdoing.
extendedMeaning: Iṣbirū wa ṣābirū, 'be patient and outlast in patience', is urged in 3:200. Ṣabbār, 'very patient', is paired with shakūr, 'very grateful' (14:5).
quranUsage: Occurs 103 times. 'Seek help through patience and prayer; Allah is with the patient (al-ṣābirīn)' (2:153). The Prophet is repeatedly told, 'be patient (fa-ṣbir)' (11:49), and the believers prayed, 'Our Lord, pour patience (ṣabran) upon us' (2:250).

primaryMeaning: The ear, and from it, hearing and knowing. Adhina is to listen and so to know, idhn is permission — letting something be known as allowed — and adhān is announcement, the call to prayer.
extendedMeaning: Adhān, 'announcement': 'an announcement (adhānun) from Allah and His Messenger to the people' (9:3). Ibrahim was told, 'proclaim (adhdhin) the pilgrimage to the people' (22:27).
quranUsage: Occurs 102 times, often as bi-idhni Allāh, 'by the permission of Allah': nothing happens without it, whether a miracle of ʿĪsā 'by My permission (bi-idhnī)' (5:110) or intercession (2:255). Ādhān, 'ears', are named among the faculties people fail to use (7:179).

primaryMeaning: To tighten and make firm, to bind strongly. Shadīd is 'severe' or 'strong', and ashudd is full strength — the age of maturity.
extendedMeaning: Musa prayed, 'strengthen (ushdud) my back through him' — through Harun (20:31).
quranUsage: Occurs 102 times. Allah is 'severe (shadīd) in punishment' (2:165). Ashadd, 'stronger', compares: hearts 'like stones or even harder (ashaddu)' (2:74). Ashuddahu, 'his full strength', marks maturity, as when orphans come of age (6:152).

primaryMeaning: To give birth. Walad is a child, wālid and wālida are father and mother, and mawlūd is one who is born.
extendedMeaning: 'Your wealth and your children (awlādukum) are a trial' (64:15).
quranUsage: Occurs 102 times. The Quran rejects that Allah has a child: 'They say, "Allah has taken a son (waladan)" — exalted is He' (2:116), and 'He neither begets nor is born (lam yalid wa lam yūlad)' (112:3). Kindness to parents is commanded next to worship of Allah: 'and to parents (wa bil-wālidayn), good treatment' (2:83).

primaryMeaning: To owe, to submit, and to be requited. Ibn Fāris says the root means yielding and submission; dayn is a debt, something owed; dīn is a way of submission — religion — and also judgment, the settling of what is owed.
extendedMeaning: 'For you your religion, and for me mine (dīni)' (109:6).
quranUsage: Occurs 101 times. Māliki yawm al-dīn, 'Master of the Day of Judgment' — the day of recompense (1:4). Dīn as religion: 'the religion (al-dīn) with Allah is Islam' (3:19), and 'There is no compulsion in religion' (2:256). Dayn, 'debt', is the subject of the longest verse, 2:282.

primaryMeaning: Ṣalāh is prayer. Classical scholars link it to supplication (duʿā') and to calling blessings on someone; others connect it to ṣalā, the lower back, bent in bowing. Ṣallā ʿalā, 'to send blessings on', is its other main use.
extendedMeaning: 'Allah and His angels send blessings (yuṣallūna) on the Prophet; O you who believe, send blessings on him' (33:56).
quranUsage: Occurs 99 times, mostly as al-ṣalāh, 'the prayer', in the command aqīmū al-ṣalāh, 'establish the prayer' (2:43), and the description of the God-conscious as those who 'establish the prayer' (2:3). 'Prayer restrains from indecency and wrongdoing' (29:45).

primaryMeaning: To keep company with someone, to accompany them. Ṣāḥib is a companion, and by extension the owner or inhabitant of something — the one who 'goes with' it.
extendedMeaning: Yusuf addressed his fellow prisoners, 'O my two companions of the prison (yā ṣāḥibayi al-sijn)' (12:39), and the Prophet reassured Abu Bakr in the cave, 'he said to his companion (li-ṣāḥibihi), "Do not grieve; Allah is with us"' (9:40).
quranUsage: Occurs 97 times, mostly as aṣḥāb, 'companions' or 'people of': aṣḥāb al-nār, 'the companions of the Fire' (2:39), aṣḥāb al-janna, 'the companions of Paradise', and aṣḥāb al-kahf, 'the people of the Cave'. Ṣāḥibukum, 'your companion', refers to the Prophet: 'your companion has not strayed' (53:2).

primaryMeaning: Brother. Akh is a brother by birth, and by extension anyone joined to another by faith, tribe or shared cause; ukht is a sister.
extendedMeaning: It carries the story of Yusuf and his brothers (12:69) and of Qabil and Habil: 'how to hide the body of my brother (akhī)' (5:31).
quranUsage: Occurs 96 times. Many prophets are introduced as 'their brother': 'to ʿĀd, their brother (akhāhum) Hud' (7:65), stressing that each prophet came from his own people. The believers are one family: 'the believers are but brothers (ikhwa)' (49:10).

primaryMeaning: To seek or want something — and to go beyond limits in seeking it. Ibtighā' is seeking; baghy is transgression and oppression; and yanbaghī, 'it is fitting', is what may properly be sought.
extendedMeaning: 'Do you seek (a-ghayra … yabghūna) other than the religion of Allah?' (3:83).
quranUsage: Occurs 96 times. Ibtighā' describes seeking a good end: 'seeking (ibtighā'a) the pleasure of Allah' (2:207), and 'that you may seek (li-tabtaghū) of His bounty' (17:12). Baghy, 'envy' or 'transgression', is why some rejected revelation (2:90) and why earlier communities divided after knowledge came to them (3:19). 'It is not fitting (mā yanbaghī) for the Most Merciful to take a son' (19:92).

primaryMeaning: To be near. Qurb is nearness, qarīb is near, and qurbā is kinship — those near by blood. Qurbān is an offering by which one seeks nearness to Allah.
extendedMeaning: 'We are nearer (aqrabu) to him than his jugular vein' (50:16). The two sons of Adam each 'offered an offering (qurbānan)' (5:27).
quranUsage: Occurs 96 times. 'When My servants ask you about Me — I am near (qarīb)' (2:186). Dhawū al-qurbā, 'relatives', are named among those owed kindness (2:83). Lā taqrabū, 'do not go near', forbids even approaching certain things — prayer while intoxicated (4:43) or unlawful sexual relations (17:32).

primaryMeaning: To love. Ibn Fāris gives three senses for the root: love and attachment, the grain (ḥabba), and a description of shortness. Classical writers link love to the grain as what settles in the heart.
extendedMeaning: Ḥabba, 'grain', appears in the parable of spending: 'like a grain (ḥabbatin) that grows seven ears' (2:261).
quranUsage: Occurs 95 times, most often in what Allah loves and does not love: 'Allah loves (yuḥibbu) those who do good' (2:195) and 'Allah does not love the transgressors' (2:190). 'If you love (tuḥibbūna) Allah, follow me; Allah will love you' (3:31). 'Those who believe are stronger in love (ḥubban) for Allah' (2:165).

primaryMeaning: To move swiftly, to swim or glide. Tasbīḥ, 'glorification', is classically explained as moving far away in declaring Allah free of every imperfection; subḥāna Allāh means 'Allah is far above that'.
extendedMeaning: The literal sense of floating or swimming describes the heavenly bodies: 'each is swimming (yasbaḥūn) in an orbit' (21:33).
quranUsage: Occurs 92 times. Subḥānahu, 'glory be to Him', answers false claims about Allah (2:116), and subḥāna alladhī asrā, 'Exalted is He who took His servant by night', opens Surah 17 (17:1). All creation glorifies Him: 'there is nothing that does not glorify (yusabbiḥu) Him with praise' (17:44).

primaryMeaning: To bow low, to humble oneself — above all, to prostrate with the forehead on the ground. Sujūd is prostration, and masjid, 'mosque', is a place of prostration.
extendedMeaning: Pharaoh's magicians, seeing the truth, 'fell down in prostration (sājidīn)' (7:120).
quranUsage: Occurs 92 times. The angels were told, 'Prostrate (usjudū) to Adam', and all did except Iblis (2:34). Al-masjid al-ḥarām, 'the Sacred Mosque', is the direction of prayer (2:144). All creation bows to Allah: 'to Allah prostrates (yasjudu) whoever is in the heavens and the earth' (13:15).

primaryMeaning: Night — the time from sunset to dawn.
extendedMeaning: Laylat al-qadr, 'the Night of Decree', is when the Quran was sent down (97:1). Surah 92 opens with an oath 'by the night when it covers' (92:1).
quranUsage: Occurs 92 times, often paired with the day as a sign: 'the alternation of night (al-layli) and day' (2:164). Allah 'causes the night to enter the day' (3:27). The night is for rest and for worship: 'stand (in prayer) through the night, except a little' (73:2).

primaryMeaning: Laysa, 'is not', is the verb of negation — denying that something is so.
extendedMeaning: On the Day of the Covenant, Allah asked, 'Am I not (a-lastu) your Lord?' (7:172).
quranUsage: Occurs 89 times. 'There is nothing like Him (laysa ka-mithlihi shay')' (42:11). 'Righteousness is not (laysa) that you turn your faces east or west' (2:177). A-laysa, 'is not…?', asks for affirmation: 'Is not Allah sufficient for His servant?' (39:36).

primaryMeaning: Most scholars derive shayṭān from shaṭana, 'to be far away' — far from the truth and from Allah's mercy. Others derive it from shāṭa, 'to burn up'. It names Satan, and any rebellious jinn or human.
extendedMeaning: Believers seek refuge before reciting: 'seek refuge in Allah from Satan the outcast' (16:98).
quranUsage: Occurs 88 times, mostly as al-shayṭān, 'Satan': 'Satan caused them to slip' (2:36), and 'do not follow the footsteps of Satan; he is to you a clear enemy' (2:168). Al-shayāṭīn, 'the devils', can include humans: 'devils (shayāṭīn) from mankind and jinn' (6:112).

primaryMeaning: To read or recite. Ibn Fāris and others note the root's older sense of gathering and joining; recitation joins letters and words together. Qur'ān, 'the recitation', is what is read and recited.
extendedMeaning: On the Day of Judgment each person is told, 'Read (iqra') your record' (17:14).
quranUsage: Occurs 88 times, mostly as al-qur'ān: 'the month of Ramadan in which the Quran (al-qur'ān) was sent down' (2:185), and 'We sent it down as an Arabic Quran (qur'ānan)' (12:2). 'Do they not reflect on the Quran?' (4:82). The first revelation begins iqra', 'Read!' (96:1).

primaryMeaning: To return. Tawba, 'repentance', is a person's turning back to Allah from sin; when Allah is the subject, tāba ʿalā means He turns to the person with mercy and accepts them.
extendedMeaning: Tawbatan naṣūḥā, 'sincere repentance', is urged in 66:8.
quranUsage: Occurs 87 times. After Adam's slip, 'his Lord turned to him (fa-tāba); He is the Accepter of repentance (al-Tawwāb), the Merciful' (2:37). The call to turn back recurs: 'turn to Allah in repentance (tūbū), all of you' (24:31), and 'Allah loves those who repent often (al-tawwābīn)' (2:222).

primaryMeaning: To remain, to last on and on. Khuld is lasting permanence, and khālid is one who stays forever.
extendedMeaning: Satan tempted Adam with 'the tree of eternity (al-khuld)' (20:120). Wildān mukhalladūn, 'youths who never age', serve in Paradise (56:17).
quranUsage: Occurs 87 times, mostly as khālidīna fīhā, 'abiding therein forever', describing both Paradise (2:25) and the Fire (2:162). Jannat al-khuld, 'the Garden of Eternity', is promised to the God-conscious (25:15).

primaryMeaning: Wealth, possessions — anything a person owns. Māl is property; amwāl its plural.
extendedMeaning: On the Day of Judgment 'neither wealth (māl) nor children will benefit' (26:88).
quranUsage: Occurs 86 times, often paired with children as a test: 'your wealth (amwālukum) and your children are a trial' (8:28). The believers strive 'with their wealth and their lives (bi-amwālihim wa anfusihim)' (4:95), and spending wealth in Allah's way is like sowing grain (2:261).

primaryMeaning: One. Aḥad is 'one' or 'anyone'; in negation it means 'no one'. Used of Allah, aḥad means absolutely One — unique, without parts and without equal.
extendedMeaning: Iḥdā, 'one of', appears in the rules for witnesses: 'if one of the two (iḥdāhumā) errs, the other can remind her' (2:282).
quranUsage: Occurs 85 times. 'Say: He is Allah, the One (aḥad)' (112:1), and 'there is none (aḥad) comparable to Him' (112:4). Most other uses mean 'anyone' or 'no one': 'do not associate anyone (aḥadan) with your Lord in worship' (18:110).

primaryMeaning: To escape, to be saved. Najāt is rescue; anjā and najjā are to save someone. Najwā, 'secret talk', is speaking aside, apart from others — on raised ground (najwa) away from the crowd.
extendedMeaning: Nuh prayed, 'save me (najjinī) and those with me of the believers' (26:118).
quranUsage: Occurs 84 times, often for Allah saving His prophets and their followers: 'We saved him (fa-anjaynāhu) and those with him in the ship' (7:64). Najwā, 'private counsel', is condemned when used for sin: 'there is no good in much of their private talk (najwāhum)' (4:114).

primaryMeaning: To forbid and to make inviolable. Ḥarām is what is forbidden — and also what is sacred, protected from violation. Ḥaram is a sanctuary, and iḥrām the sacred state of the pilgrim.
extendedMeaning: Makkah is 'a secure sanctuary (ḥaraman āminan)' (28:57). Ḥurum describes pilgrims in iḥrām (5:1).
quranUsage: Occurs 83 times. Ḥarrama, 'He forbade', sets out what is unlawful: 'He has forbidden (ḥarrama) you only carrion, blood, the flesh of swine…' (2:173). Al-masjid al-ḥarām, 'the Sacred Mosque', and al-ashhur al-ḥurum, 'the sacred months', are protected from violation (2:144, 5:2).

primaryMeaning: To be level and even — equal on all sides. Sawā' is 'equal' or 'the same'; sawwā is to make something even, to fashion it in proportion; and istawā is to rise and settle firmly, or to become fully formed.
extendedMeaning: Sawā' al-sabīl, 'the level way', is the right path (2:108).
quranUsage: Occurs 83 times. 'It is the same (sawā'un) to them whether you warn them or not' (2:6). Lā yastawī, 'they are not equal', compares opposites (4:95). Sawwā describes creation: 'who created and fashioned in proportion (fa-sawwā)' (87:2). Istawā describes Allah turning to the heaven (2:29) and rising over the Throne (7:54).

primaryMeaning: Kayfa, 'how?' — a question about the state or manner of something.
extendedMeaning: Fa-kayfa, 'then how will it be…?', points to a coming moment of reckoning (3:25).
quranUsage: Occurs 83 times. It often asks with wonder or reproach: 'How (kayfa) can you disbelieve in Allah when you were dead and He gave you life?' (2:28). It invites reflection on the fate of earlier peoples: 'see how (kayfa) was the end of the deniers' (3:137), and on creation: 'Do they not look at the camels, how (kayfa) they were created?' (88:17).
